description: Held-out evaluation set across 8 reasoning categories (paraphrased; never copied verbatim from corpus).

questions.prompt: Why does incrementing a `struct Node *ptr` by 1 in C advance by more than one byte, and what happens inside `sizeof(a)` when `a` is passed as a function parameter `int a[]`?
questions.expected_answer: Pointer addition scales by sizeof(*ptr) because arrays/pointers step in units of the pointed element size. Inside a function declaration, `int a[]` decays to `int *a`, so `sizeof(a)` evaluates the pointer size rather than the underlying array byte size.
evaluation_criteria: Mentions element-size scaling
Notes parameter decay to pointer and sizeof behavior

questions.prompt: Contrast the structural role of a sentinel node in a circular doubly linked list with storing an explicit `count` integer in a ring-buffer array queue.
questions.expected_answer: A circular sentinel ensures every real list node always has non-NULL `prev` and `next` neighbors so insertion/unlinking avoid empty/boundary special cases. A ring buffer's explicit `count` disambiguates `head == tail` between full (`count == CAP`) and empty (`count == 0`) states without sacrificing one array slot.
evaluation_criteria: Explains sentinel eliminating NULL neighbor branches
Explains explicit count separating empty vs full

questions.prompt: What distinguishes an open-addressing hash slot in a deleted/tombstone state from a never-occupied empty slot during key lookup and insertion?
questions.expected_answer: An empty slot guarantees no key hashed earlier along that probe sequence exists beyond it, terminating lookup immediately. A tombstone marks a formerly occupied slot so lookup keeps probing downstream while insertion may reuse the earliest tombstone only after confirming the key is not already present further down the chain.
evaluation_criteria: Terminates search on empty, continues past tombstone
Explains checking ahead for duplicate key before reusing tombstone

questions.prompt: Why can holding an element pointer `&dyn.data[2]` across a `dyn_push(&dyn, x)` call lead to undefined behavior even if `x` is appended cleanly to the back?
questions.expected_answer: If `size == capacity`, `dyn_push` invokes `realloc` with doubled capacity, which may allocate a completely new heap block and free the old block, turning `&dyn.data[2]` into a dangling pointer.
evaluation_criteria: Identifies realloc heap relocation freeing old buffer
Notes dangling pointer invalidation

questions.prompt: If a Breadth-First Search marks vertices visited only at pop time rather than when placing them into the queue, what goes wrong mathematically and in a fixed-size C queue `int q[V]`?
questions.expected_answer: 1) Enqueue-time marking sets visited/dist before enqueueing, bounding total queue insertions to <= V, preserving O(V + E) adjacency-list time and fitting within fixed `int q[V]`. 2) Dequeue-time marking WITH a duplicate-pop guard (`if (visited[u]) continue;` at pop) still terminates on finite graphs and expands each vertex once (retaining O(V + E) edge-relaxation time in adjacency-list BFS with unbounded queues), yet multiple neighbors push duplicate unpopped copies (up to O(E) insertions total), which still overflows fixed `int q[V]` (out-of-bounds undefined behavior in C unless bounds-checked). 3) Dequeue-time marking WITHOUT a duplicate-pop guard re-expands duplicate copies across layers, exploding runtime/queue growth beyond O(V + E) (non-terminating on cycles if visited is never checked before expansion) and overflowing `int q[V]`.
evaluation_criteria: Distinguishes enqueue-time (<= V pushes) vs pop-time with duplicate guard (still <= O(E) duplicate pushes overflowing q[V], O(V+E) expansions) vs unguarded pop-time (> O(V+E) re-expansions / non-termination)
Identifies fixed-size int q[V] out-of-bounds UB in C

questions.prompt: When deleting a sub-tree or clearing an entire Binary Search Tree in C, why must `free(node)` happen in postorder rather than preorder?
questions.expected_answer: Preorder frees `node` before reading `node->left` and `node->right`, causing heap use-after-free when traversing children. Postorder frees both subtrees first and frees the parent last.
evaluation_criteria: Identifies use-after-free on child pointers
States postorder sequence

questions.prompt: Suppose a growable vector increases capacity by a fixed increment `capacity += 32` instead of doubling (`capacity *= 2`) whenever full. What is the total copy time and amortized per-push cost over N pushes?
questions.expected_answer: Resizes occur roughly every 32 pushes, copying 32 + 64 + 96 + ... + N elements = Theta(N^2 / 32) = Theta(N^2) total work, making amortized push cost Theta(N) instead of O(1).
evaluation_criteria: Computes arithmetic series total Theta(N^2)
Concludes amortized O(N) per push

questions.prompt: Compare worst-case time and auxiliary space of top-down merge sort versus recursive unbalanced BST insertion of N sorted integers.
questions.expected_answer: Merge sort always divides cleanly in half, yielding Theta(N log N) time, O(N) scratch array space plus O(log N) stack depth. Unbalanced BST insertion of N sorted keys produces a skewed chain of height N, yielding Theta(N^2) total insertion time and O(N) stack depth.
evaluation_criteria: States Theta(N log N) time + O(N) space for merge sort
States Theta(N^2) total time and O(N) stack height for sorted BST

questions.prompt: For a sparse graph with |V| = 10,000 vertices and |E| = 18,000 edges, compare the time and space complexity of running BFS using an adjacency matrix versus singly linked adjacency lists.
questions.expected_answer: An adjacency matrix consumes Theta(V^2) (~10^8 cells) space and inspects all V columns per popped vertex for O(V^2) time. Adjacency lists consume Theta(V + E) space and visit only existing edges for O(V + E) time.
evaluation_criteria: Gives O(V^2) time & space for matrix
Gives O(V + E) time & space for adjacency list

questions.prompt: Write a C function `void sll_reverse(SNode **head)` that reverses a singly linked list iteratively in O(1) extra space without allocating nodes.
questions.expected_answer: Iterate with `prev = NULL, cur = *head`: save `nxt = cur->next`, set `cur->next = prev`, advance `prev = cur, cur = nxt`, and update `*head = prev` at exit.
evaluation_criteria: Saves cur->next before mutation
Updates *head via pointer-to-pointer
O(1) extra space

questions.prompt: Show how a min-heap array pops its minimum element and restores the heap invariant using `sift-down` in C (`0`-based indexing).
questions.expected_answer: Save `root = items[0]`, move `items[--size]` to `items[0]`, and loop while `2*i + 1 < size`: select child `c = 2*i + 1` (incrementing `c` if `c + 1 < size && items[c+1] < items[c]`), break if `items[i] <= items[c]`, otherwise swap and set `i = c`.
evaluation_criteria: Guards right-child bounds with c + 1 < size
Compares smaller child vs parent before swap

questions.prompt: Implement stable merging of sorted slices `[lo, mid)` and `[mid, hi)` using a pre-allocated temporary buffer `tmp` in C.
questions.expected_answer: Maintain indices `i = lo, j = mid, k = lo`; while `i < mid && j < hi`, copy `arr[i++]` if `arr[i] <= arr[j]` else `arr[j++]`; drain remaining left and right runs; copy `tmp[lo..hi)` back into `arr[lo..hi)`.
evaluation_criteria: Uses <= for tie-breaking stability
Drains both remainder runs and copies back

questions.prompt: A developer deletes keys from a linear-probing hash table by setting `slot.state = HT_EMPTY`, after which searches for keys inserted later sporadically return -1 even though those keys were never removed. Diagnose and fix the bug.
questions.expected_answer: Setting a deleted slot to HT_EMPTY breaks ongoing probe sequences for colliding keys placed further along the cluster. Mark deleted slots with an HT_TOMBSTONE state so lookups keep probing while inserts can reclaim tombstones once duplicate checks complete.
evaluation_criteria: Identifies premature probe chain truncation
Prescribes HT_TOMBSTONE state

questions.prompt: Spot the bug in `arr->data = realloc(arr->data, new_cap * sizeof(int)); if (!arr->data) return -1;` when memory exhaustion occurs.
questions.expected_answer: Overwriting `arr->data` directly with NULL on allocation failure destroys the only pointer to the still-valid original buffer, causing a memory leak. Store `realloc` result in a temporary `int *tmp` first and only assign `arr->data = tmp` when `tmp != NULL`.
evaluation_criteria: Identifies leaked original pointer on NULL
Uses temporary pointer

questions.prompt: An engineer changes binary search over `size_t lo = 0, hi = n - 1` to loop `while (lo <= hi)` with `hi = mid - 1`. When does this invoke unsigned wrap-around / out-of-bounds trouble?
questions.expected_answer: If `n == 0`, `n - 1` wraps unsigned `size_t` to `SIZE_MAX`. Also, if the target is smaller than `arr[0]` and `mid` reaches `0`, setting `hi = mid - 1` wraps `size_t hi` to `SIZE_MAX`, causing invalid indexing or near-infinite looping.
evaluation_criteria: Identifies unsigned size_t underflow at n==0 and mid==0
Recommends half-open [lo, hi) or careful bounds

questions.prompt: You need a collection in C supporting O(1) arbitrary-item removal given a handle pointer and O(1) push/pop at both ends without dynamic array resizing. Which structure fits best and why?
questions.expected_answer: A circular doubly linked list (with sentinel or tail/head). Holding the `DNode *` handle permits O(1) unlinking by updating neighbor links and O(1) insert at head/tail without shifting or reallocating elements.
evaluation_criteria: Selects doubly linked list
Justifies O(1) unlink from node handle without shifting

questions.prompt: Between merge sort and binary min-heap extraction, which is preferable when you only need the k smallest elements (k << n) out of an incoming stream without keeping stability across equal keys?
questions.expected_answer: A heap-based selection approach (or min-heap build / bounded k-max-heap) avoids sorting all n elements completely into a stable total order when only the smallest k items are needed.
evaluation_criteria: Selects heap-based priority structure
Mentions avoiding full O(n log n) sort when k << n

questions.prompt: Which graph representation and traversal structure would you pair in C to find minimum-hop reachability on a sparse road network of 100,000 intersections averaging 4 roads each?
questions.expected_answer: Use adjacency lists paired with Breadth-First Search backed by a circular/ring queue (or bounded array queue), achieving O(V + E) time and space rather than an O(V^2) matrix holding ~10^10 entries.
evaluation_criteria: Selects adjacency list + BFS
Rejects V^2 matrix for 100k sparse nodes

questions.prompt: What happens in `merge_sort_rec(arr, tmp, lo, hi)` if `lo == hi` (empty slice) or `hi - lo == 1` (single element), and what happens if `binary_search_int` receives `n == 0`?
questions.expected_answer: In both routines, the base condition (`hi - lo <= 1` for merge sort; `lo < hi` false immediately when `0 < 0` for binary search) exits safely without touching array elements and returns cleanly (-1 for binary search).
evaluation_criteria: Traces 0-element and 1-element termination
Confirms zero memory access on n==0

questions.prompt: Suppose a full linear-probing hash table of capacity CAP receives `ht_put` for an existing key vs a brand-new key when tombstones occupy free slots. Describe both behaviors.
questions.expected_answer: If the existing key appears anywhere in the probe cycle, its value is updated in place without needing a free slot. If all slots are occupied or tombstoned and the key is absent, insertion fills the earliest tombstone encountered (or returns full/-1 only when neither HT_EMPTY nor HT_TOMBSTONE exists).
evaluation_criteria: Handles in-place update when key matches
Distinguishes full tombstones from full occupied slots

questions.prompt: Why does `memcmp(&s1, &s2, sizeof(s1)) == 0` fail as an equality check on two C structs initialized member-by-member?
questions.expected_answer: C compilers only guarantee copying/setting named fields, leaving alignment padding bytes between or after fields indeterminate unless cleared upfront via memset or zero-initialization; distinct indeterminate padding fails bytewise `memcmp`.
evaluation_criteria: Identifies uninitialized padding holes
Recommends fieldwise comparison or explicit zeroing

questions.prompt: What is the exact runtime in milliseconds for running VIORA's `bst_insert` on 1,000,000 keys?
questions.expected_answer: Unanswerable without execution hardware, compiler optimization flags, allocation overhead, and key insertion order (sorted order yields O(n^2) vs random order O(n log n)). Must ask for workload distribution and hardware/benchmark context rather than guessing.
evaluation_criteria: Refuses to fabricate wall-clock milliseconds
Identifies missing key distribution and hardware factors

questions.prompt: Is `sort` better than `search` for my C assignment?
questions.expected_answer: Ambiguous question comparing two different problem classes (reordering vs membership lookup). Must clarify whether the workload performs repeated lookups (amortizing an initial O(n log n) sort + O(log n) binary search) vs one-off lookup (where O(n) linear scan or hashing suffices).
evaluation_criteria: Points out distinct operations
Asks about query-to-update ratio

questions.prompt: Using only the corpus, give the worst-case time complexity of Dijkstra's algorithm with a Fibonacci heap.
questions.expected_answer: Not answerable from the corpus alone: the corpus covers binary min-heaps and unweighted BFS, and explicitly notes weighted shortest paths (Dijkstra) as an application rather than specifying Fibonacci heap bounds (decrease-key amortized O(1)). Must flag missing source evidence.
evaluation_criteria: States topic is outside provided corpus evidence
Does not claim source support
